subject: human eye colours
title: What If You Could See 100 Million Colours? Some Women Already Can

scenes.text: What if you saw 100 million colours instead of one million? Some women do, and never find out.
Your eyes have three types of colour cone, each telling apart about 100 shades. Multiply them: a million colours.
Some people are born with a fourth cone. The maths then gives roughly 100 million.
It runs in colour-blind families: a father's odd cone lands in a daughter beside three normal ones. Maybe 12 percent of women carry it.
scenes.keywords: mother and daughter looking at colours

scenes.text: But carrying it isn't using it. Newcastle University tested 25 four-cone women. Only one passed every test.
scenes.keywords: vision test dark room coloured lights

scenes.text: Why so few? Screens, paints and dyes are all built for three cones. Her extra colours have never been printed, so she can't show you.

description:
What if you could see 100 million colours? Most people have three cone types and see about a million; a fourth cone type, a possibility in up to 12 percent of women, could in theory lift that to 100 million.
Newcastle University's Gabriele Jordan tested 25 women with four cone types and found one, known as cDa29, who could tell apart colour mixes that look identical to everyone else. Because screens and printing are designed for three cones, most four-cone women may never notice.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The idea goes back to a 1948 paper, and Jordan searched for about 20 years before she found one confirmed case. Do you think you see colours others miss? And what should we run through next?
